title: the bridge
hook: five days, a whole army of builders, and the stories people added later

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bridge, promised. The ocean said it couldn't change what it was, but it would hold up whatever was built, and it named Nala as the builder. Did you build with something that won't change? Today, they build. Day six hundred thirty-six.

Nala steps forward, and what he says is quietly funny. The ocean is right, he tells Rama. I'm Vishvakarma's son, and I have my father's skill. I can build this. Then he adds, more or less: nobody asked me, so I didn't mention it. An army has been staring at an impossible sea for days, and the one person who could solve it was standing in the crowd, waiting for someone to ask. Then the work begins.
screen: `NALA STEPS FORWARD.` → `NOBODY ASKED ME.` → `THE WORK BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki loves the noise of it. The monkeys and bears pour into the forests and tear up trees by the thousand: palms, ashokas, flowering trees of every kind. They drag whole boulders down from the hills and heave them into the water with a sound like thunder. Some hold measuring lines while others lay the stones. And he counts the days. Fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. In five days it's done: a bridge a hundred yojanas long and ten wide, running straight across the sea. The gods come and watch from the sky, Valmiki says, amazed, and then the army crosses to the shore of Lanka. Now, two things you may have heard that aren't in Valmiki. One is the squirrel. A little squirrel rolls in the sand and shakes it onto the bridge to help, and Rama strokes its back, and the stripes are his fingers. The other is the stones that float because Rama's name is written on them. Both come from later retellings and oral tradition, and devotees tell them as lessons in devotion: no gift is too small, and the name carries weight. But they're later additions, and it's worth knowing which is which. Today, the line of shoals and sandbanks between Rameswaram in India and Mannar in Sri Lanka is called Rama Setu, Rama's bridge, in Hindu tradition. People hold different views about what that chain of shoals is, and those arguments are still going on. What Valmiki gives is simpler: a whole people, five days, one bridge.
screen: `TREES, BOULDERS AND THUNDER.` · `FIVE DAYS, A HUNDRED YOJANAS.` · `THE SQUIRREL CAME LATER.` · `RAMA SETU TODAY.` · then, large: `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ONE BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Think of the people around you this week: at work, at home, in your neighborhood. Is there a Nala among them, someone with a skill nobody has thought to ask about? Picture their face. Hold them in mind kindly, and let the question rest: what could I ask them? Then come back to the breath, in and out, one stone at a time. The bell holds the time.
The bridge. Setu. Built in five days by an army of monkeys and bears under Nala, a hundred yojanas long, carried by the ocean that promised to hold it up.
Your line: the bridge. Today, ask one quiet person what they're good at. You may find a Nala. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Rameswaram and Dhanushkodi on India's southeastern coast, linked by tradition to the bridge, and the squirrel's story is a common children's tale.

fork.setup: you're Nala. the army has stared at the sea for days, and you know you could build a bridge. nobody has asked. what do you do?
options: wait to be asked, then say so.
keep quiet; it's not your place.
fork.reveal: Nala speaks once the ocean names him, and says he didn't mention his skill because nobody asked.

original.note: Sanskrit setubandha: the binding, or building, of the bridge; also the name given to the place.

trapdoor: what you thought: the bridge was built by Rama's power alone.
what it means: a whole army built it in five days, under Nala, on an ocean that promised to bear it.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki counts it day by day; the squirrel and the floating named stones are later, beloved additions.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 22 (Nala's offer; the building of the bridge in five days; the crossing)

notes: Nala's remark that he wasn't asked, so he didn't speak of his skill: paraphrased; confirm.
The daily counts (14, 20, 21, 22, 23 yojanas) and the bridge's size (100 by 10 yojanas): confirm against the vulgate.

The squirrel story and the floating stones inscribed with Rama's name are described as later retellings, not Valmiki; a Keeper may want to name specific sources (e.g. regional Ramayanas, oral tradition).
Rama Setu / Adam's Bridge: the script says only that many Hindus call the shoals Rama Setu and that views differ; it takes no position on their origin.
Rama's worship of Shiva at Rameswaram is left out; it is not in the vulgate's account of the building.
